clue.text: Spoiling old woman wearing jewellery

indicators.note: A person wearing something is inside it, so the letters standing for the wearer go within the other lot.

parts.note: bling is flashy, conspicuous jewellery
o = old, the usual one-letter shortening
w = woman, the letter on the lavatory door

explanation.surface: An elderly woman decked out in her jewellery, being thoroughly indulged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoiling' reads as pampering a grandmother and wants the other sense, ruining something through your own carelessness. The old woman is two of the crossword's commonest single letters, standing side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Spoiling → BLOWING: to blow a chance or an interview is to spoil it by your own doing, the colloquial sense of wrecking something you had.

clue.text: General hides a cigarette in vegetation

indicators.note: To hide a thing is to put it out of sight inside something bigger, so one set of letters is swallowed by another.

parts.note: Robert E Lee, the Confederate commander, is the crossword's default general
the word itself, taken straight
fag is everyday British slang for a cigarette

explanation.surface: A general concealing a smoke somewhere in the undergrowth.
explanation.walkthrough: A cigarette is a fag in Britain and a general is Lee — two conventions stacked in one short clue, which is why the middle is so hard to see. 'In' only joins; 'hides' is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: vegetation → LEAFAGE: leafage is the collective word for all the leaves a plant or a wood carries, which is what vegetation mostly amounts to.

clue.text: Snakes and ladders board in Fiji now ends being flipped

indicators.note: The end of a word is its final letter, and each word in the run gives up only that.
Flipped over, a collected string comes out in the opposite order to the one it went in.

parts.note: the final letter of each of those five words, taken in clue order

explanation.surface: A snakes-and-ladders board being turned upside down somewhere in Fiji.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snakes and ladders' is a board game the eye refuses to split, and the definition is the first word of it on its own. Fiji and 'now' are in the clue only for the letters they end with.
explanation.definitionFit: Snakes → WINDS: a lane that snakes through the hills winds through them, both verbs for a course that keeps bending.

clue.text: Woman's brown back has a fracture

indicators.note: Something turned back faces the way it came, so this piece is entered in the opposite order.

parts.note: tan is a shade of brown, turned about

indicators.note: A fracture breaks a thing into parts that no longer sit where they did, so those letters are to be rearranged.

parts.note: the four letters of 'has a' rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman's suntanned back turns out to be fractured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brown back' asks for a colour reversed, not a part of the body, and the two little words after it are fodder rather than grammar. The name is Russian, the pet form of Natalia.
explanation.definitionFit: Woman → NATASHA: a woman's given name, Russian in origin and common in English, so the clue defines by example rather than by synonym.

clue.text: Modern cricketer gets final boundary of series

parts.note: batter is the gender-neutral term that has lately replaced batsman in cricket

indicators.note: The final thing in a word is its last letter, and only that letter is wanted.

parts.note: the last letter of 'boundary'

explanation.surface: A cricketer hitting a four with the last ball of the series.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boundary' looks like more cricket and is only a word to take a letter from — a four or a six is a boundary, and none of that matters. Cricket really has swapped batsman for batter, and setters noticed.
explanation.definitionFit: series → BATTERY: a battery of tests, questions or lawsuits is a whole series of them delivered one after another.

clue.text: Chooses a pet with no tail, a bit tame in afterthought

indicators.note: An animal's tail is at its rear end, so the word loses the letter at its back.
A bit of a word is a small part of it, and the smallest part offered here is its opening letter.
'In' puts what has just been named inside what comes next.

parts.note: the word itself, taken straight
the pet is a dog, and the word has been docked
ps = postscript, the afterthought tacked onto the end of a letter
the opening letter of 'tame'

explanation.surface: Someone picking a docked, rather placid pet, apparently as an afterthought.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma is placed to mislead: 'a bit tame' belongs with the afterthought that follows it, not with the pet it sits beside. Docking a word's tail takes one letter and never more.
explanation.definitionFit: Chooses → ADOPTS: to adopt a stray, a policy or a child is to choose it and take it on as your own.

clue.text: Elizabeth Reef — our secret signature

indicators.note: Something secret is kept out of sight inside whatever surrounds it, so the letters lie buried in the words as written.

parts.note: the letters run on consecutively from inside the first word, straight across the dash

explanation.surface: A pact signed in secret between the two of us, out at Elizabeth Reef.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Signature' here is musical: a time signature is the count of beats in a bar, and a hyphenated pair of numbers is how one is written. The dash makes a gap the eye trusts, and the buried run crosses it.
explanation.definitionFit: signature → THREE-FOUR: a time signature names the beats in a bar, and three-four is the waltz's, three beats to each bar.

clue.text: Managed royal position

parts.note: to run a business is to manage it, and this is the past tense
the royal wanted is the man on the throne

explanation.surface: A post at court that somebody once ran.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Managed' is past tense, so the piece it gives has to be past tense too — that agreement is often the way into a charade. The definition is the last word, where a three-word clue usually keeps it.
explanation.definitionFit: position → RANKING: your ranking is the position you hold in a league or a list, the place rather than the title.

clue.text: Sand dune got moved — plausible?

indicators.note: Letters that have been moved are no longer where they started, so this lot is to be reordered.

parts.note: to sand a surface is to smooth it
the seven letters of 'dune got' rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone claims a sand dune has shifted overnight, and the claim is being weighed up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sand dune' is one thing on the surface and the answer cuts it in half, taking the first word as a verb. Said of a person, plausible means convincing in a way you are being warned about.
explanation.definitionFit: plausible? → SMOOTH-TONGUED: of a person, plausible means glib and persuasive in the suspect way a smooth talker is, not simply believable.

clue.text: Novelist in a state penning article

indicators.note: To pen animals is to shut them in an enclosure, so these letters are boxed inside the others.

parts.note: MN is Minnesota's two-letter postal code
an is one of the three English articles

explanation.surface: A novelist in a flap while writing an article.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penning' is the writing word the surface needs and the enclosing word the wordplay needs, which is why the clue reads so smoothly. Thomas Mann wrote Death in Venice and The Magic Mountain.
explanation.definitionFit: Novelist → MANN: the surname of Thomas Mann, the German author of Buddenbrooks and The Magic Mountain, a novelist named by his family name alone.

clue.text: Playing tuba in Rome with another instrument

indicators.note: To play with a thing is to knock it out of its settled order, so the letters beside the word are not to be read as they stand.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A tuba being played in Rome alongside a second instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing' is the ideal anagram word for a clue about instruments, because it means what a musician does and what a shuffler does. Ten letters sit in plain sight with only their order as disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: another instrument → TAMBOURINE: a hand drum hung with jingles, and 'another' does the work of saying it is not the tuba just mentioned.

clue.text: Cold musician's unlimited drink

indicators.note: Something unlimited has had its limits taken off, and a word's limits are the letters at either end.

parts.note: c = cold, the letter on the tap
the musician is a bassist, stripped of the letter at each end

explanation.surface: A chilly musician drinking without limit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unlimited' is worth learning beside 'limits': the first and last letters of a word are its limits, and both go at once. The drink is French, a blackcurrant liqueur.
explanation.definitionFit: drink → CASSIS: crème de cassis is the French blackcurrant liqueur poured into white wine to make a kir.

clue.text: Live report of where Prince William's crown might be?

indicators.note: A report of something is an account of how it sounds, so what follows is to be heard rather than read.

parts.words: where Prince William's crown might be?
parts.note: Prince William is first in line to the British throne, so the crown is waiting on the heir

explanation.surface: A live news report asking where Prince William keeps his crown.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is doing real work: it flags that the whole phrase is a joke arrived at by sound, not a fact about the royal jewels. British radio and television have used this phrase for broadcasting since the 1920s.
explanation.definitionFit: Live → ON THE AIR: a programme on the air is going out as it happens, which is exactly what live means of radio or television.

clue.text: Subject's alter ego 'Gary' seen outside pub

indicators.note: To alter a thing is to change the way it is arranged, so these letters are to be rearranged.
What is seen outside stands round the edge of something else, which goes in the middle.

parts.note: the seven letters of 'ego' and 'Gary' rearranged, ready to be opened up
PH is public house, the mark used for a pub on a British map

explanation.surface: Somebody's alter ego, a man called Gary, spotted standing outside a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alter ego' is so fixed a phrase that the eye will not break it, and the setter wants only its second half. The quotation marks round the name are surface dressing and carry no instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Subject → GEOGRAPHY: a subject on a school timetable, standing alongside history and maths as one of the standard ones.

clue.text: Sing loudly following party in open area outside town

indicators.note: What follows a thing comes along after it, so this piece is written below the other in a down entry.

parts.note: the Greens are Britain's environmental party
to belt out a number is to sing it at full volume

explanation.surface: Belting out a song after a party held on land just beyond the edge of town.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are ordinary words doing unusual jobs — one a political party rather than a colour, the other a way of singing rather than something worn. In British planning law this land is protected from building.
explanation.definitionFit: open area outside town → GREEN BELT: the green belt is the ring of countryside round a British city that planning law keeps free of development.

clue.text: Relatives stealing £1,000 records …

indicators.note: A thief takes a thing in and keeps it about them, so these letters go inside the others.

parts.note: sons are relatives
a grand is a thousand pounds and G is what a grand shortens to

explanation.surface: Family members caught making off with a thousand pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: The eye glues '£1,000' to 'records' and reads them as records worth a thousand pounds, which is where the definition hides. The ellipsis runs on into the next clue, but neither needs the other to solve.
explanation.definitionFit: records → SONGS: on a chart or a playlist the two words name the same tracks, the recording standing for the piece that was recorded.

clue.text: … by backing group holding note

indicators.note: Backing a thing means going the other way along it, so in an across entry the letters are read from the right.
To hold something is to keep it within your grasp, so one set of letters closes round the other.

parts.note: a set is a group of things taken together
mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A record made by a backing group holding a single long note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing group' reads as the band behind a singer and splits into an instruction plus a word. The definition is the little word at the front, which the ellipsis dresses up as grammar.
explanation.definitionFit: by → TIMES: a room described as ten by twelve is ten times twelve, so 'by' is how multiplication is spoken aloud.

clue.text: During chaotic reign, no good prince becomes smoker?

indicators.note: What happens during an event happens inside it, so this piece goes within the letters around it.
Chaos is the absence of order, so the letters beside the word are not in the order they are to be read in.
'No' in front of a thing takes it away, so the letter it names is not available.

parts.note: anagram fodder, five letters before anything is removed
g = good, and this is the letter leaving the fodder
Prince Hal is the young Henry V of Shakespeare's history plays, the crossword's standard prince

explanation.surface: Midway through a disorderly reign, a worthless prince takes up smoking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No good prince' is one insult on the surface and three separate instructions underneath, with the comma placed to hide the seam. The shuffled letters end up wrapped round the prince rather than beside him.
explanation.definitionFit: smoker? → INHALER: both name something that draws substance into the lungs, and the question mark admits the everyday word is a device rather than a person.

clue.text: Make president replace politician with court after tricks

indicators.note: To replace one thing with another is to take the first out and stand the second in the gap it leaves.
In an across entry what comes after something is written to its right, so the altered word lands at the end.

parts.note: a con is a trick or a swindle
Donald Trump, a US president, taken before anything is done to the name
MP is a Member of Parliament, the British politician — these are the letters coming out
ct = court, as it appears in a street address — these are the letters going in

explanation.surface: A president swapping a politician for a courtroom in the wake of some swindles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make' sits at the front looking like an order given to the president, and it is the definition. The president is never named: you supply the surname yourself, then operate on it.
explanation.definitionFit: Make → CONSTRUCT: to construct something is to make it by fitting parts together, the building sense of make rather than the forcing one.

clue.text: Boss to drink more rum

indicators.note: Rum is an old British adjective meaning odd or peculiar, and something odd is not in its proper order.

parts.note: to sup is to drink, still ordinary usage in the north of England
the four letters of 'more' rearranged

explanation.surface: The boss knocking back yet more rum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' is trap and instruction at once: the spirit on the surface, the old adjective meaning odd underneath. Any drink named at the end of a clue is worth testing as an anagram word.
explanation.definitionFit: Boss → SUPREMO: a supremo is the person in overall charge of an organisation, the boss the other bosses answer to.

clue.text: Growth of bird has head increase by a factor of 20

indicators.note: The head of a word is its first letter, and that is the letter being operated on.

parts.note: a vulture is the bird, taken before anything happens to it
read as a Roman numeral the opening letter is five; twenty fives are a hundred, which is Roman C

explanation.surface: A bird whose head has grown twenty times bigger.
explanation.walkthrough: The arithmetic here is Roman, not decimal: a letter is a number, and multiplying it hands you a different letter. 'Growth' is a laboratory word in this clue, not a garden one.
explanation.definitionFit: Growth → CULTURE: a culture is the growth of bacteria or cells raised deliberately in a dish, the biologist's sense of the word.

clue.text: Matches 50 and 88? Pointless at first

parts.note: L is fifty in Roman numerals

indicators.note: A compass has points, and something pointless has lost one.

parts.note: 88 written out as a pair of them
E is east, a point of the compass, and 'at first' says the leading letter is the one going

explanation.surface: Numbers being called at bingo, the early ones worth nothing at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Matches' is a plural noun here, not a verb, and the things it names are struck rather than played. The question mark after 88 admits that writing it out as a pair is the solver's move.
explanation.definitionFit: Matches → LIGHTS: asking a stranger for a light means asking for a match, so a light is one of them and lights are several.

clue.text: Reforming c-capital punishment

parts.note: the stray letter the stammer leaves standing in front
hanging was the form capital punishment took in Britain, abolished in 1965

explanation.surface: A nervously delivered demand that the death penalty be reformed.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen makes the opening letter look like a stutter, and that is the whole disguise: it is an extra letter parked in front of a word. Britain hanged its condemned right up to abolition.
explanation.definitionFit: Reforming → CHANGING: to reform a law or an institution is to change it, and both words here are present participles doing the same job.

clue.text: Sell bicycle part to the audience

indicators.note: Something delivered to an audience is heard rather than seen, so the word is to be judged by its sound.

parts.note: the part of a bicycle you push round with your foot

explanation.surface: Flogging bicycle components to a crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: Two spellings, one sound, and the definition is the single word at the front. The words are unrelated: one comes from the Latin for foot, the other from a pedlar's pack.
explanation.definitionFit: Sell → PEDDLE: to peddle goods is to sell them by carrying them about, the street trader's kind of selling.

clue.text: Welshman taking part in Normandy landings

indicators.note: To take part in something is to be a part of it, so what is wanted is part of the words that follow.

parts.note: the letters run consecutively out of the end of the first word and into the second

explanation.surface: A Welshman who went ashore on D-Day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking part in' does double duty: joining the invasion on the surface, pointing at a run of letters underneath. A real place and a real event sit side by side, which is what keeps the join invisible.
explanation.definitionFit: Welshman → DYLAN: a Welsh first name, worn by the Swansea poet Dylan Thomas, so a man of Wales is what it names.

clue.text: Low church, perhaps York, returned English food

indicators.note: Letters that have returned come back the way they went, so in an across entry they are read from the right.

parts.note: to feel low is to feel blue
ch = church, the abbreviation used on maps
York is one example of a see, the district a bishop governs, and the word comes back the other way
e = English

explanation.surface: A plain Anglican service, perhaps at York, where the English food was sent back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low church' is a real phrase for plain Anglican worship, and the clue splits it down the middle. 'Perhaps' is not decoration: it flags that York is one example of the thing meant, not the thing itself.
explanation.definitionFit: food → BLUE CHEESE: Stilton, Roquefort and gorgonzola are blue cheeses, veined with mould and very much eaten, so the general word covers them.

clue.text: Praise God for all to hear

indicators.note: Said out loud for everybody, so the word is to be taken by its sound rather than its spelling.

parts.note: the Lord is God, and said aloud it comes out spelt another way

explanation.surface: Praising God openly.
explanation.walkthrough: Four words, and three of them are the sound instruction — the clue is a definition and a homophone marker with almost nothing in between. In most English accents the two spellings differ only on paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Praise → LAUD: to laud someone is to praise them, a formal verb that survives mainly in 'much lauded'.

clue.text: Demonstrate in favour of cricket's longest format

parts.note: pro means in favour of, the opposite of anti
a Test match is the five-day international game, the longest form cricket is played in

explanation.surface: Marching in support of the five-day game.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface campaigns in favour of something and the answer is what you do against it, so the two halves pull in opposite directions. A Test is cricket's five-day international, set beside the one-day and twenty-over versions.
explanation.definitionFit: Demonstrate → PROTEST: to demonstrate in the street is to protest, the marching sense of the verb rather than the proving one.

clue.text: Oppose noble queen

parts.note: a count is a continental nobleman
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the late queen's cipher

explanation.surface: A call to stand against a noble queen.
explanation.walkthrough: ER stood on British postboxes and helmets for seventy years and is the crossword's default queen. 'Noble' looks like an adjective attached to the queen and is a nobleman in his own right.
explanation.definitionFit: Oppose → COUNTER: to counter a move or an argument is to oppose it, meeting it with something of your own.
